That's the one thing I hate about murder statistics whenever they are brought up. They make overly broad statements without acknowledging the legal and factual intricacies of coming up with these numbers.

Some questions to consider: How many of these were cases of involuntary manslaughter/homocide/depraved heart? What number of cases are reported v. unreported? What cases resulted in acquittals? What about missing persons reports that could also affect these numbers or juvenile murder rates?

There are so many uncertain factors that it is impossible to come up with an accurate estimate of murder rates and thus they should not be given so much weight.

A murder is a murder, regardless if the case is solved or not or what the reason for it was. They usually don't rule someone murdered unless there is evidence of it, like a body. So someone who ran away or went missing wouldn't be part of these statistics. There really isn't much uncertainty about this, someone was either murdered or they weren't.

But what about general intent v. specific intent homocides? If there's an overwhelming number of involuntary manslaughter cases caused by multiple DUI drivers in an area, then that's a very different situation from a serial killer who rapes, tortures, and kills the same number of infants (unrealistic, extreme example to accentuate point I'm trying to make). Not all murders are equal. Circumstances have a big role to play in the conclusions you can draw.
